analysis.investment_thesis: Ashwini Container Movers fails both legs of the Magic Formula — ROE of 0.72% signals near-zero return on capital, while a ~7.4% earnings yield (1/P/E of 13.6x) falls well short of the 12%+ threshold I require for a "cheap" stock. A bad business at a mediocre price is not a bargain.
key_strengths: Modest valuation at 13.6x P/E provides some downside cushion vs. deep overvaluation
High promoter holding of 66.67% aligns owner interests with shareholders
FII + DII combined 14.6% ownership suggests some institutional validation of the name
key_risks: ROE of 0.72% is catastrophically low — barely above zero, failing the quality test decisively
Road transport is capital-intensive and commoditized — trucks, fuel, and driver costs destroy ROIC
Geographic concentration in Maharashtra/Gujarat limits scale and pricing power
red_flags: ROE 0.72% — the Magic Formula requires ROIC >20%; this is 28x below that threshold
Earnings yield ~7.4% (1/13.6x P/E) — below Greenblatt's 12% minimum; not cheap enough to offset poor quality
Micro-cap (INR 208 Cr) in a fragmented commodity transport sector — no visible moat
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula asks two questions simultaneously: is this a good business, and is it cheap? Ashwini fails on quality in emphatic fashion. An ROE of just 0.72% in a capital-intensive trucking business means the company is deploying shareholder equity into trucks, terminals, and working capital and earning virtually nothing in return. In Greenblatt's framework, ROIC must exceed 20-25% for a business to rank in the top decile — Ashwini's implied ROIC is likely in low single digits at best, placing it firmly in the bottom tier. Road transport in India is a hyper-fragmented, low-margin sector with no pricing power, making sustained improvement structurally difficult.

On valuation, the P/E of 13.6x implies an earnings yield of ~7.4% — marginally above a risk-free rate but well below the 12-15% EBIT/EV I look for as a "cheap" signal. The stock is neither cheap enough to compensate for poor capital returns, nor good enough as a business to merit a premium. With INR 208 Cr market cap, thin institutional sponsorship outside promoters, and no identifiable competitive moat, there is no Magic Formula case here. I would need to see ROIC above 15% and earnings yield above 12% simultaneously to get interested — both metrics would need to roughly double from current levels.
